planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chuan Xiong is a cool-climate herb traditionally grown at higher elevation in Sichuan and prefers cooler summer conditions than the Gulf South provides.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chuan Xiong is a cool-climate herb traditionally grown at higher elevation in Sichuan and prefers cooler summer conditions than the Gulf South provides. Finely divided, celery-like aromatic foliage and small umbels of white flowers grow from a knobby, strongly aromatic rhizome that is the part harvested and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, where it has long been valued for supporting healthy circulation. Historically cultivated at elevation in Sichuan province, it performs best where summers stay relatively mild and struggles with prolonged heat and humidity, making it a better fit for a cooler mountain or northern garden than a hot, humid Gulf Coast bed. Harvest and dry the rhizomes in fall after the foliage dies back, typically after one to two seasons of growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reference

planting.note: Start transplants indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and set out in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Shen is grown chiefly for its distinctive brick-red roots, harvested after the plant has grown for at least one full season.

directions: Start transplants indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and set out in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Shen is grown chiefly for its distinctive brick-red roots, harvested after the plant has grown for at least one full season. Soft, hairy, deeply veined leaves and spikes of violet-blue, two-lipped flowers typical of the sage family top a clumping perennial whose real value lies underground, in thick, branching roots with a distinctive brick-red exterior that is a cornerstone herb of traditional Chinese medicine, long used to support healthy circulation. It is easy to grow in ordinary garden conditions much like culinary sage relatives, tolerating a range of soils, and the showy flowers are an added bonus for pollinators even where the roots are not harvested. Dig roots for use in fall after two or more years of growth, when they have reached a useful size, and cut back spent flower stalks after bloom to keep the clump tidy.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hardy rubber tree is extremely adaptable and tolerates heat, cold, drought, and urban pollution better than most shade trees.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hardy rubber tree is extremely adaptable and tolerates heat, cold, drought, and urban pollution better than most shade trees. Glossy, elm-like leaves that exude fine, elastic latex threads when torn give this tree both its common name and its most reliable identifying trait, and its bark, the source of du zhong, is one of the most widely used tonic herbs in traditional Chinese medicine, traditionally associated with supporting bone and joint health. A tough, adaptable, pest- and disease-resistant tree with no serious ornamental drawbacks, it makes a reliable, low-maintenance shade or street tree independent of any medicinal use, and is the only surviving species in its ancient plant family. Bark for medicinal use is typically harvested from mature trees using sustainable partial-strip techniques that allow the bark to regenerate rather than felling the tree.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reference

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; She Chuang Zi is grown as a cool-season annual and is harvested for its seed once the flat seed umbels turn brown and dry.

directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; She Chuang Zi is grown as a cool-season annual and is harvested for its seed once the flat seed umbels turn brown and dry. Finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat-topped clusters of small white flowers, typical of the carrot family, are followed by small, ribbed, aromatic seeds that are the part collected and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, historically applied topically for skin conditions. An easy, weedy annual related to Queen Anne's lace and wild carrot, it grows quickly from seed in ordinary garden soil with minimal care and self-sows readily if seed heads are left standing. Harvest seed umbels once they have dried and turned brown on the plant, and thresh the small seeds free before storing in a cool, dry place.

planting.note: Mount on bark or rock, or pot in coarse orchid bark mix, in bright, indirect light in a warm, humid location; Shi Hu is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a greenhouse or indoor orchid.

directions: Mount on bark or rock, or pot in coarse orchid bark mix, in bright, indirect light in a warm, humid location; Shi Hu is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a greenhouse or indoor orchid. Slender, jointed, cane-like stems bear narrow leaves and small, fragrant, pale yellow-green to white flowers, but the plant is prized chiefly for its thick, mucilage-rich fresh or dried stems, one of the most highly valued tonic herbs in traditional Chinese medicine and historically among the most expensive due to its slow growth and vulnerability to overharvesting in the wild. Cultivated commercially on rock faces or tree bark in parts of China to relieve pressure on rapidly declining wild populations, it can be grown similarly in a home setting mounted on bark or grown in an orchid-appropriate bark mix with good humidity and air movement. Water regularly during active growth, allow the mount or mix to dry somewhat between waterings, and maintain high humidity and warmth year-round for the best growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
